asserted_unverified.qualifier_as_published: *based on workflows for System One tasks (proof)

asserted_unverified.claim: two orders of magnitude faster and more efficient, at similar levels of intelligence on System One tasks compared to existing LLMs
asserted_unverified.note: 'System One tasks' is a vendor-defined task class. No task list is published, so the comparison set cannot be reconstructed by a third party.

The vendor's own FAQ separately carries the question 'Can Jev still get things wrong?'. The claim as headlined and the claim as qualified in the FAQ are not obviously the same claim. A typed output space constrains the FORM of an output; whether it constrains the CORRECTNESS of an output is exactly the thing an independent evaluation would have to establish, and none exists.

measured.note: We do not adjudicate which figure the vendor intends. We record that a reader relying on a secondhand summary would have quoted numbers the primary source does not carry. This is the failure mode the card exists to catch.
measured.observed: The commissioning brief carried '20-200x faster, 40-400x cheaper'. The live homepage states '193.6x Faster, 444.6x Cheaper'. The vendor's own launch post instead says 'two orders of magnitude faster and more efficient'. Three different magnitude statements for the same product.
measured.question: Do the figures in the brief that prompted this card match the primary source?

measured.note: Recorded as a dated fact about the public record only. We assert no intent, no causal link to the absence of published evaluations, and no criticism of the argument, which is made in good faith and is substantially one we share. A reader may hold both that public benchmarks are gameable and that vendor-internal figures are uncheckable; this card measures only the second.
measured.observed: Post 'Lies, Damned Lies, and Benchmarks', dated 'Sep 11, 2026' — four days before the Jev launch — argues that public evaluations are systematically gamed: 'A benchmark inevitably gets benchmaxxed when people building the model can optimize for a public eval score.'
measured.question: Has the vendor published a position on third-party benchmarking?

payload.method: Enumerate the vendor's own public surface and ask, for each artifact a third party would need in order to check a performance claim, whether that artifact exists. Every row is the result of a fetch we performed, with the URL and the UTC timestamp of that fetch. Absence is only recorded as ABSENT where it was established from an index the vendor itself publishes (sitemap.xml, a registry search API) — never from a URL we guessed.
payload.recheck_trigger: Re-run when sitemap.xml gains a docs, model-card or evaluation URL, when a model card appears on a public registry, or when self-serve access opens.

state_vocabulary.ASSERTED_UNVERIFIED: a party asserts this; no independent check was run by us or, so far as we could find, by anyone
state_vocabulary.FETCH_FAILED: we attempted the fetch and it did not return usable bytes; the attempt is recorded
state_vocabulary.MEASURED: we fetched a primary source and the row records what the bytes said
state_vocabulary.NOT_CHECKED_THIS_RUN: carried into this card from a referring summary and not independently checked here

what_this_card_does_not_say: It does not say the vendor's figures are wrong. It says they are uncheckable from public sources today.
It does not say the product does not work.
It does not grade, rank, score or certify TypeSafe AI or Jev.
It does not assert that the vendor is obliged to publish an evaluation.
